nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the gentleman thief and the imperial adventure
literary_identity: Writer of fiction and verse; the creator of A. J. Raffles, the gentleman burglar, and the brother-in-law of Arthur Conan Doyle.
biography: Born Ernest William Hornung at Middlesbrough on 7 June 1866; he was sent to Australia for his health in 1884 and returned to London in 1886, publishing Under Two Skies in 1892. The Amateur Cracksman (1899) introduced Raffles; The Shadow of the Rope (1902), Stingaree (1905) and The Crime Doctor (1914) followed. He married Constance Doyle in 1893, served in the First World War, and died at Saint-Jean-de-Luz, France, on 22 March 1921.
literary_profile: Hornung created A. J. Raffles, the first gentleman thief in English fiction and the direct ancestor of the modern heist story and the charming criminal, and he wrote the finest of the imperial adventure novels of the 1890s in The Shadow of the Rope. His work gave the detective story its mirror image and made the criminal into a hero of style.
stylistic_characteristics: The first-person narrative by the admiring accomplice; the aristocratic criminal with a code of honour; the cricket match and the country house as settings for the crime; the epigrammatic dialogue of the club; the sudden violence under the surface of the gentleman's world.
intellectual_concerns: The gentleman and the criminal; the public school code and its corruption; the empire and the colonial return; money and the idle rich; loyalty between men.
historical_significance: E. W. Hornung created the first gentleman thief in English fiction and the ancestor of the modern heist story: Raffles gave the detective genre its mirror image, made the criminal into a hero of style, and opened the way for the moral ambiguity of the twentieth-century crime novel.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the boys' adventure of the sea and the wilderness
literary_identity: Writer for boys; the author of The Coral Island, one of the founding books of the boys' adventure story of empire.
biography: Born Robert Michael Ballantyne in Edinburgh on 24 April 1825, the son of the printer and novelist James Ballantyne; he went to Canada as a clerk with the Hudson's Bay Company at sixteen, returned to Scotland in 1847, and made his name with The Coral Island (1858). Hudson Bay (1848), Martin Rattler (1858), The Dog Crusoe (1860), The Gorilla Hunters (1861) and dozens more followed. He died in Rome on 8 February 1894.
literary_profile: Ballantyne wrote the founding books of the boys' adventure story of empire: The Coral Island invented the desert-island adventure for boys, and his Canadian and African tales created the formula of the young hero, the wilderness and the trial of manhood that Rider Haggard, Stevenson and Kipling all inherited.
stylistic_characteristics: The documentary detail drawn from first-hand experience; the episodic adventure of the voyage and the island; the direct address to the boy reader; the moral lesson folded into the action; the plain, energetic, instructive prose.
intellectual_concerns: The wilderness and the frontier; the empire and the fur trade; the boy's initiation into manhood; race and the encounter with the native; natural history and the observation of the world.
historical_significance: R. M. Ballantyne wrote the founding books of the boys' adventure story of empire: The Coral Island invented the desert-island adventure for boys and it was the book that Stevenson, Haggard and Kipling all read as children, making it the origin of the imperial adventure novel.

literary_identity: Writer for boys; the most prolific author of naval and colonial adventure stories in the mid-Victorian period.
biography: Born William Henry Giles Kingston in London on 28 February 1814; he spent some years in Portugal in the wine trade, and after the success of Peter the Whaler (1851) and The Three Midshipmen (1873) he devoted himself to writing for boys, producing well over a hundred books. He was a founder of the Young Men's Christian Association in London and died at Willesden on 5 August 1880.
literary_profile: Kingston was the most prolific writer of boys' sea stories in the mid-Victorian period and did more than anyone to establish the naval adventure as a genre: his midshipmen, his storms and his sea battles gave the boy reader the Navy as a moral institution and shaped the sea story that Marryat and Conrad both worked in.
stylistic_characteristics: The voyage as the organising structure; the technical language of sail and seamanship; the storm and the sea battle; the moral improvement of the young officer; the patriotic digression and the improving address.
intellectual_concerns: The Navy and the empire; duty, discipline and the chain of command; the sea as a test of character; the contact with the colonial world; the Christian mission.
historical_significance: W. H. G. Kingston was the most prolific writer of boys' sea stories in the mid-Victorian period and the writer who made the naval adventure into a genre: his midshipmen and his sea battles gave the boy reader the Navy as a moral institution and shaped the sea story that Conrad inherited.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the historical adventure of empire
literary_identity: Novelist and war correspondent; the most popular writer of historical adventure for boys in the Victorian age and the great populariser of the imperial version of history.
biography: Born George Alfred Henty at Trumpington on 9 December 1832; he served in the Crimean War and as a war correspondent in the Austro-Italian war, the Abyssinian expedition and the Ashanti war. After the success of Out on the Pampas (1871) he produced some eighty historical adventure novels, from The Young Buglers (1880) to With the Allies to Pekin (1904). He died on board his yacht in Weymouth harbour on 16 November 1902.
literary_profile: Henty was the most popular writer of historical adventure for boys in the Victorian age and the great populariser of the imperial version of history: his eighty novels taught a generation the history of the British Empire as a series of campaigns in which a young man could take part, and they fixed the formula of the historical adventure novel that lasted until the Second World War.
stylistic_characteristics: The young hero placed at the centre of a real historical campaign; the meticulous military and topographical detail; the episodic campaign narrative; the didactic preface and the imperial moral; the plain, reportorial prose of the correspondent.
intellectual_concerns: The empire and the imperial idea; war and the heroic code; the historical past as a school of manhood; race and the colonial encounter; the British character and its destiny.
historical_significance: G. A. Henty was the most popular writer of historical adventure for boys in the Victorian age and the great populariser of the imperial version of history: his eighty novels taught a generation the history of the empire as a series of campaigns and fixed the formula of the historical adventure novel for the next fifty years.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the comic fantasy of the body-swap
literary_identity: Novelist and humorist; the pseudonym of Thomas Anstey Guthrie, the inventor of the comic body-swap novel in English.
biography: Born Thomas Anstey Guthrie in London on 8 August 1856; he was educated at King's College School and Trinity Hall, Cambridge, trained as a barrister, and made his name with Vice Versa (1882). The Tinted Venus (1885), A Fallen Idol (1886), The Pariah (1889), The Talking Horse (1892) and The Brass Bottle (1900) followed. He wrote for Punch and died in London on 10 March 1934.
literary_profile: F. Anstey invented the comic body-swap novel in English: Vice Versa, in which father and son change places, was a bestseller on both sides of the Atlantic and founded a comic formula that has never gone out of use, and The Brass Bottle gave the modern djinn story its English form.
stylistic_characteristics: The comic premise carried to its logical extreme; the narrative of embarrassment and social catastrophe; the invented magic object and its domestic consequences; the light, dry, ironic prose; the satire of the Victorian school and family.
intellectual_concerns: The school and the family; the generation gap and the reversal of authority; the commercial middle class and its ambitions; the classical past in the modern home; the comedy of the impossible.
historical_significance: F. Anstey invented the comic body-swap novel in English: Vice Versa was a bestseller on both sides of the Atlantic, founded a comic formula that has never gone out of use, and The Brass Bottle gave the modern djinn story its English form.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the comic diary and the operetta
literary_identity: Actor, singer and writer; the co-author of The Diary of a Nobody and the principal comedian of the Gilbert and Sullivan operas.
biography: Born George Grossmith in London on 9 December 1847, the son of the entertainer George Grossmith; he created the patter roles in The Sorcerer, H.M.S. Pinafore, The Pirates of Penzance, Patience, Iolanthe, Princess Ida, The Mikado, Ruddigore, The Yeomen of the Guard and The Gondoliers. With his brother Weedon he wrote The Diary of a Nobody (1892), first serialised in Punch; his comic lectures and his autobiography A Society Clown (1888) followed. He died in Folkestone on 1 March 1912.
literary_profile: George Grossmith was the greatest English comic performer of his age and, with his brother Weedon, the author of The Diary of a Nobody, the funniest English comic novel of the nineteenth century and the founding text of the suburban comedy of manners.
stylistic_characteristics: The mock diary form with its deadpan self-importance; the suburban setting of brick and respectability; the running gag and the recurring minor character; the comic understatement of catastrophe; the parody of the Victorian diary and the memoir.
intellectual_concerns: The suburb and the lower middle class; respectability and its anxieties; social aspiration and its humiliation; the family and the domestic routine; the comic dignity of the ordinary man.
historical_significance: George Grossmith was the greatest English comic performer of his age and, with Weedon Grossmith, the author of The Diary of a Nobody: the funniest English comic novel of the century and the founding text of the suburban comedy of manners, which has never been out of print and which founded the comic suburb in English fiction.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the public poet and the national narrative
literary_identity: Poet, professor and translator; the most widely read American poet of the nineteenth century and the maker of the national historical poem.
biography: Born in Portland, Maine, on 27 February 1807; he taught modern languages at Bowdoin and at Harvard, where he held the Smith chair from 1836 to 1854. Voices of the Night (1839), Evangeline (1847), The Song of Hiawatha (1855), The Courtship of Miles Standish (1858) and Tales of a Wayside Inn (1863) made him the most popular poet in the English-speaking world. He died in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 24 March 1882, the first American poet honoured with a bust in Poets' Corner.
literary_profile: Longfellow was the most widely read American poet of the nineteenth century and the maker of the national historical poem: Evangeline and Hiawatha gave American literature its epics of the Acadian exile and the Native American past, and his public poetry made the poet a national institution in a way no American writer had been before.
stylistic_characteristics: The long narrative poem in regular tetrameter; the historical and legendary subject nationalised; the simile drawn from the natural world; the moral sentiment of the public poet; the plain, melodious, accessible line.
intellectual_concerns: The American past and the national memory; the Native American and the vanishing race; the Puritan inheritance; the sea and the New England coast; death and the consolation of fame.
historical_significance: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was the most widely read American poet of the nineteenth century and the maker of the national historical poem: Evangeline and The Song of Hiawatha gave American literature its epics and made the poet a national institution, and his influence on the public poetry of the English-speaking world was unmatched.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the abolitionist poet and the New England idyll
literary_identity: Poet and abolitionist; the most important anti-slavery poet in America and the poet of the New England farm.
biography: Born in Haverhill, Massachusetts, on 17 December 1807 to a Quaker farm family; he edited the Middlesex Standard and the abolitionist Pennsylvania Freeman, was mobbed for his views in 1835, and published Voices of Freedom (1846), Snow-Bound (1866) and The Tent on the Beach (1867). He was a founder of the Republican Party in Massachusetts and died at Hampton Falls, New Hampshire, on 7 September 1892.
literary_profile: Whittier was the most important anti-slavery poet in America and one of the two or three finest poets of the New England farm: Snow-Bound is the great American poem of the rural household, and his abolitionist verse gave the movement its hymns and its moral authority.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, ballad-like quatrain and the domestic idyll; the Quaker plainness of speech; the abolitionist appeal and the moral indignation; the New England landscape and the fireside; the dialect poem of the rural poor.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery and the abolitionist cause; the New England farm and the vanishing rural world; the Quaker conscience; death and the immortality of the household; poverty and the dignity of labour.
historical_significance: John Greenleaf Whittier was the most important anti-slavery poet in America: his abolitionist verse gave the movement its hymns and moral authority, and Snow-Bound is the great American poem of the rural household and the fireside.
